activities.title: Setting Up a Computer
activities.description:
In this activity, you will look inside a computer, fit its main parts, and connect its devices to the right ports.

Tip: Walk around the computer to see its back, where the cables connect.
activities.subject: Computer Science

steps.title: Observe

confirm.title: Ready to Move On?
confirm.content: Are you ready to move to the next exercise?

captions.text: A computer system is made of parts that work together. Some parts take data in, some process it, and some give information out.
The monitor is an output device. It shows us text, pictures, and video.
The keyboard and the mouse are input devices. We use them to type, to point, and to click.
The system unit holds the parts that process and store data. Let's lift off its cover and look inside.
The large circuit board is the motherboard. Every part connects to it, so the parts can share power and data.
This is the central processing unit, or CPU. It carries out instructions and does calculations. It is the brain of the computer.
These are the memory modules, called RAM. RAM holds the programs and data you are using right now. When the power goes off, RAM is emptied.
The storage drive keeps your files and programs, even when the computer is switched off.
The power supply unit changes electricity from the wall socket into the power that the parts need.
Now let's turn the system unit around. At the back are the ports, where the cables connect.
Each kind of cable has its own shape of port. A plug only fits the port that matches it, and only one way round.
The monitor cable goes into the HDMI port. The keyboard and mouse go into USB ports. The network cable goes into the LAN port.
Connect every cable first, and switch on the power last. Before you open a computer, always switch it off and unplug it.
Select Next to continue.

steps.description: Observe the parts of a computer system, what each one does, and how they connect.

dragItems.holdCaption:
CPU:
the processor. Hold it by its edges. Line up the gold triangle with the triangle on the socket, then lower it in gently. Never press on the pins.

RAM:
the computer's working memory. Hold it by its edges. Line up the notch with the key in the slot, then press down firmly until both clips click.

Storage drive:
an M.2 solid state drive. Slide it into the M.2 slot at a small angle, then press it down and fix it with its screw.

HDMI cable:
it carries picture and sound from the computer to the monitor. It has a flat plug with two slanted corners, so it fits only one way.

Keyboard USB plug:
the keyboard's cable ends in a flat, rectangular USB plug. Push it into any USB port, with the plastic tongue facing the right way.

Mouse USB plug:
the mouse also uses a USB plug. It goes into another USB port, next to the keyboard.

Network cable:
an Ethernet cable connects the computer to the school network. Its plug clicks into the LAN port. Press the clip to take it out.

Power cable:
it brings electricity from the wall socket to the power supply unit. Connect it last, after every other cable.

activities.title: Circulatory System
activities.description: In this activity, you will explore the circulatory system. Tip: Move the device around to see the circulatory system from different angles.
activities.subject: Biology

steps.title: Observe

confirm.title: Ready to Move On?
confirm.content: Are you ready to move to the next exercise?

captions.text: You require oxygen to survive. The cells in your body use oxygen to help process the energy and nutrients into energy that cells can use.
Your lungs take in the oxygen, and then oxygen moves into your blood.
But how does the oxygen in blood get to the rest of the body? Think of the circulatory system as the body’s delivery system.
It transports nutrients, gases, wastes, and other substances throughout the body.
The circulatory system includes your heart, blood, and blood vessels.
Heart muscle contractions pump blood out of the heart to the body.
When the muscles relax, blood from the body enters the heart.
There are three types of blood vessels that help blood travel. They are arteries, veins, and capillaries.
Arteries carry oxygen-rich blood away from the heart.
Veins transport blood that contains carbon dioxide to the lungs where it is re-oxygenated and sent back to the heart via the pulmonary veins
Capillaries are tiny passages that connect the arteries and veins.
All these parts of your circulatory system work together to help move blood through your body.
Select next to continue.

captions.text: The human eye is a fascinating and complex organ. In fact, your eye is just like a camera. It cannot function without light.
When your eye sees an image, light reflects off the object and enters the eye.
Because the front part of the eye is curved, it bends the light, creating an upside-down image on the retina.
The brain turns the image right side up helping you to focus on the object.
Each of the eye's distinct parts has a specific responsibility helping you to take in information and process the world around you.
Select next to continue.

dragItems.holdCaption:
Retina:
a thin layer of tissue that lines the back of the eye that captures light and helps to translate images to the brain

Sclera:
the white outer layer of the eyeball that protects and supports your eye

Choroid:
the vascular layer of the eyeball between the retina and the sclera that brings oxygen and nutrients to the eye

Iris:
the colorful part of the eye that helps to regulate the amount of light that enters the retina

Cornea:
a transparent dome that covers the iris and the pupil that helps the eye focus as light passes through

Optic nerve:
a bundle of nerve fibers located in the back of the eye that relays messages from the retina to your brain

Lens:
a clear curved disc that sits behind the iris that changes shape to bring things into focus

Pupil:
the black circle in the center of the iris that lets light enter the eye

steps.title: Observe

confirm.title: Ready to Move On?
confirm.content: Are you ready to move to the next exercise?

captions.text: Each part of your respiratory system has an important role in moving materials around your body.
As you inhale air through your nose or mouth, it follows a path down the pharynx to the trachea, to the bronchi, and then to the lungs.
The path is reversed when you exhale.
Your diaphragm sits under your lungs. It contracts and relaxes as you take air in and out, helping your body to regulate air pressure.
The respiration process exchanges gases between the body and its environment.
When you breathe air into and out of your lungs, it allows your respiratory system to take in oxygen and eliminate carbon dioxide.
The oxygen is then used to carry out life processes.
Select next to continue.

dragItems.holdCaption:
Oxygen:
a gas that enters the body during inhalation

Capillary:
microscopic, one cell-wall thick blood vessel where exchange of materials occurs between blood and body cells

Alveoli:
microscopic sacs, or pouches, where oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange

Wall of alveolus:
a thin wall covered in capillaries that allows a high rate of gas exchange between the alveoli and blood

Bronchi:
two narrow tubes that lead into the lungs

Lungs:
the main organs of the respiratory system

Trachea:
a tube that is held open by C-shaped rings of cartilage that connects the pharynx to the bronchi

Carbon dioxide:
a gas that leaves the body during exhalation
